70316.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70316.question_text:
Identify the life cycle type of the following crops and explain your reasoning:
Maize (Zea mays), Onion (Allium cepa), and Cassava (Manihot esculenta).
70316.explanation:
Maize (Zea mays) is an annual crop because it completes its life cycle (germination, growth, flowering, seed production, and death) within one growing season.

Onion (Allium cepa) is a biennial crop because it completes its life cycle in two growing seasons: vegetative growth in the first year and flowering/seed production in the second year.

Cassava (Manihot esculenta) is a perennial crop because it grows for several years, producing harvestable roots annually without dying after a single season.

70317.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70317.question_text:
Classify the following crops into their respective botanical families:
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), Cabbage (Brassica oleracea), and Rice (Oryza sativa).
70317.explanation:
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) belongs to the Solanaceae family.

Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) belongs to the Fabaceae (Leguminosae) family.

Cabbage (Brassica oleracea) belongs to the Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) family.

Rice (Oryza sativa) belongs to the Poaceae (Gramineae) family.

70318.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70318.question_text: Describe a practical method to determine the texture of a given soil sample. Include the steps and expected observations for sandy, loamy, and clayey soils.
70318.explanation:
Method: Ribbon Test (Field Texture Test)

  1. Take a handful of moist (not wet) soil and knead it into a ball.
  2. Press the soil between your thumb and forefinger to form a ribbon.
  3. Observe the length and feel of the ribbon before it breaks.

Expected Observations:
  • Sandy soil: Forms a weak ball that crumbles easily; no ribbon forms.
  • Loamy soil: Forms a firm ball; ribbon breaks at 2–5 cm; feels smooth but slightly gritty.
  • Clayey soil: Forms a sticky, pliable ball; ribbon extends beyond 5 cm; feels smooth and sticky.

70319.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70319.question_text:
Design a simple field experiment to demonstrate the effect of vegetative cover on soil erosion. Include:
(a) Materials required,
(b) Procedure,
(c) Expected observations, and
(d) Conclusion.
70319.explanation:
(a) Materials Required:

  • Two identical trays or shallow boxes (e.g., 50 cm × 30 cm × 10 cm)
  • Garden soil
  • Grass or plant seedlings
  • Watering can with a fine rose
  • Measuring cylinder
  • Stopwatch

(b) Procedure:
  1. Fill both trays with the same amount of soil to the same level.
  2. Plant grass or seedlings in one tray (Tray A) and leave the other tray bare (Tray B).
  3. Place both trays on a slight slope (e.g., 10°).
  4. Using the watering can, simulate rainfall by pouring 500 ml of water over each tray from the same height and rate.
  5. Collect the runoff water from each tray in separate containers and measure the volume.
  6. Observe the soil loss in each tray.

(c) Expected Observations:
  • Tray A (with vegetation): Less runoff water collected; minimal soil loss; water appears clearer.
  • Tray B (bare soil): More runoff water collected; significant soil loss; water appears muddy.

(d) Conclusion:

Vegetative cover reduces soil erosion by protecting the soil surface from the impact of raindrops, improving water infiltration, and binding soil particles with roots.

70320.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70320.question_text:
Outline the steps for treating maize seeds with hot water to control seed-borne diseases. Include:
(a) Temperature and duration,
(b) Procedure, and
(c) Precautions.
70320.explanation:
(a) Temperature and Duration:

  • Temperature: $52°C$ to $55°C$
  • Duration: 10 to 15 minutes

(b) Procedure:
  1. Fill a container with water and heat to the required temperature ($52°C$–$55°C$).
  2. Place maize seeds in a permeable bag or cloth.
  3. Immerse the bag in the hot water for 10–15 minutes.
  4. Remove the seeds and spread them on a clean surface to cool and dry.
  5. Store or plant the treated seeds.

(c) Precautions:
  • Use a thermometer to monitor water temperature accurately.
  • Avoid overheating, as temperatures above $55°C$ may kill the seeds.
  • Ensure seeds are completely dry before storage to prevent mold growth.
  • Do not treat seeds intended for consumption.

70321.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70321.question_text: Describe how to implement an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategy for controlling fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) in a maize farm. Include at least four IPM components.
70321.explanation:
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Strategy for Fall Armyworm:

  1. Monitoring and Scouting:
    • Regularly inspect maize fields (at least twice weekly) for signs of fall armyworm eggs, larvae, or damage (e.g., ragged leaves, frass).
    • Use pheromone traps to monitor adult moth populations.

  2. Cultural Control:
    • Practice crop rotation with non-host crops (e.g., legumes) to disrupt the pest’s life cycle.
    • Plant early-maturing maize varieties to escape peak pest infestations.
    • Remove and destroy crop residues after harvest to eliminate overwintering sites.

  3. Biological Control:
    • Encourage natural enemies such as parasitic wasps (e.g., Cotesia marginiventris), predatory beetles, and birds.
    • Apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Nucleopolyhedrovirus (NPV) as biological pesticides.

  4. Chemical Control (Last Resort):
    • Use selective insecticides (e.g., emamectin benzoate, chlorantraniliprole) only when economic thresholds are exceeded.
    • Apply insecticides early in the morning or late in the evening to target larvae and minimize harm to beneficial insects.
    • Rotate insecticides to prevent resistance development.

70322.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70322.question_text:
Compare the drip irrigation and sprinkler irrigation systems under the following headings:
(a) Water efficiency,
(b) Suitability for crops,
(c) Initial cost, and
(d) Labor requirement.
70322.explanation:
FeatureDrip IrrigationSprinkler Irrigation
(a) Water EfficiencyHigh water efficiency (90–95%) as water is delivered directly to the root zone, minimizing evaporation and runoff.Moderate water efficiency (70–80%) due to evaporation and wind drift losses.
(b) Suitability for CropsIdeal for row crops (e.g., vegetables, orchards), high-value crops, and areas with water scarcity.Suitable for a wide range of crops (e.g., cereals, grasses, vegetables) and large fields.
(c) Initial CostHigh initial cost due to tubing, emitters, filters, and automation systems.Lower initial cost compared to drip, but may require pumps and pipes.
(d) Labor RequirementLow labor requirement once installed, but requires regular maintenance (e.g., cleaning emitters).Moderate labor requirement for moving sprinklers and system maintenance.

70323.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70323.question_text:
Design a step-by-step protocol for preventing post-harvest losses in tomatoes. Include methods for:
(a) Harvesting,
(b) Handling,
(c) Storage, and
(d) Transportation.
70323.explanation:
(a) Harvesting:

  1. Harvest tomatoes at the breaker stage (when color changes from green to pink) for better shelf life.
  2. Use sharp knives or scissors to cut the fruit from the vine, leaving a short stem attached.
  3. Avoid harvesting during the hottest part of the day to reduce heat stress.
  4. Sort tomatoes by size and maturity to prevent bruising of ripe fruits.

(b) Handling:
  1. Handle tomatoes gently to avoid bruising or puncturing.
  2. Use clean, dry containers (e.g., plastic crates or baskets) lined with soft materials (e.g., paper or cloth).
  3. Avoid stacking containers too high to prevent compression damage.
  4. Remove any damaged or diseased fruits immediately to prevent spoilage spread.

(c) Storage:
  1. Store tomatoes at $10°C$–$15°C$ with 85–90% relative humidity for short-term storage (1–2 weeks).
  2. For long-term storage, use controlled atmosphere storage with reduced oxygen ($3–5%$) and elevated carbon dioxide ($2–3%$).
  3. Avoid refrigeration below $10°C$ to prevent chilling injury (e.g., loss of flavor, texture).
  4. Store tomatoes away from ethylene-producing fruits (e.g., bananas, apples) to delay ripening.

(d) Transportation:
  1. Use refrigerated trucks or well-ventilated vehicles for long-distance transport.
  2. Pack tomatoes in single layers or use dividers to prevent movement and bruising.
  3. Cover the load with a tarpaulin to protect from direct sunlight and dust.
  4. Monitor temperature and humidity during transit to maintain quality.

70324.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70324.question_text:
Describe how to prepare and apply compost tea as an organic fertilizer in a vegetable farm. Include:
(a) Materials required,
(b) Preparation steps,
(c) Application method, and
(d) Benefits.
70324.explanation:
(a) Materials Required:

  • Well-decomposed compost
  • Clean water (preferably rainwater or dechlorinated water)
  • Large bucket or container (e.g., 20-liter capacity)
  • Permeable bag or cloth (e.g., burlap sack)
  • Aeration device (e.g., aquarium pump or manual stirring)
  • Strainer or fine mesh
  • Sprayer or watering can

(b) Preparation Steps:
  1. Fill the permeable bag with 1–2 kg of well-decomposed compost.
  2. Place the bag in the bucket and fill with 10 liters of water.
  3. Aerate the mixture by stirring manually or using an aquarium pump for 24–48 hours to encourage microbial activity.
  4. Remove the bag and strain the liquid through a fine mesh to remove solid particles.
  5. Dilute the compost tea with water at a ratio of 1:5 (tea:water) before application.

(c) Application Method:
  1. Apply compost tea to the soil around the base of plants or as a foliar spray using a sprayer.
  2. For foliar application, spray early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid leaf burn.
  3. Apply every 2–4 weeks during the growing season.

(d) Benefits:
  • Provides readily available nutrients to plants.
  • Enhances soil microbial activity, improving nutrient cycling.
  • Suppresses soil-borne diseases through beneficial microorganisms.
  • Improves soil structure and water retention.
  • Reduces the need for synthetic fertilizers, promoting sustainable farming.

70325.subject: Crop Husbandry And Horticulture
70325.question_text:
Propose a climate-smart agriculture (CSA) plan for a smallholder maize farmer in Northern Ghana. Include strategies for:
(a) Drought resilience,
(b) Soil health improvement,
(c) Pest and disease management, and
(d) Income diversification.
70325.explanation:
(a) Drought Resilience:

  • Adopt drought-tolerant maize varieties (e.g., Obatanpa, Omankwa).
  • Practice conservation agriculture (e.g., minimum tillage, mulching) to improve soil moisture retention.
  • Use rainwater harvesting techniques (e.g., tied ridges, zaï pits) to capture and store water.
  • Implement agroforestry (e.g., planting Faidherbia albida) to provide shade and reduce evapotranspiration.

(b) Soil Health Improvement:
  • Apply organic manure (e.g., compost, farmyard manure) to improve soil fertility and structure.
  • Practice crop rotation with legumes (e.g., cowpea, groundnut) to fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Use cover crops (e.g., mucuna, lablab) to prevent erosion and add organic matter.
  • Reduce chemical fertilizer use and adopt integrated soil fertility management (ISFM).

(c) Pest and Disease Management:
  • Adopt Integrated Pest Management (IPM) to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides.
  • Use biological control agents (e.g., Trichogramma wasps for stem borers).
  • Plant trap crops (e.g., napier grass) to divert pests from maize.
  • Monitor weather patterns to predict pest outbreaks (e.g., fall armyworm during dry spells).

(d) Income Diversification:
  • Integrate livestock (e.g., poultry, goats) to provide manure and additional income.
  • Adopt agroforestry (e.g., shea nut, cashew) for long-term income.
  • Produce value-added products (e.g., maize flour, animal feed) to increase profitability.
  • Participate in climate-smart cooperatives for access to markets and finance.
